analytic.title: Framework for the design of Java firm real-time systems oriented to the generation of timing behaviour models

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This work proposes a framework for the design of complex Java firm real-time applications that run on embedded systems. The framework simplifies the real-time patterns included in the Real-Time Specification for Java (RTSJ) with the aim of systematizing the process of modelling and configuring the scheduling of real-time object-oriented applications. Moreover, with the proposed strategy, the designer of a real-time application can automatically obtain the timing behaviour model of the application, which is used to analyse and/or configure its schedulability so that it can be executed on an embedded system meeting its firm real-time requirements. The framework supports the design of applications whose real-time tasks interact asynchronously with non real-time ones.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: The continuous reduction in the cost of hardware and technology has led to embedded systems equipped with powerful processors, operating systems, communication networks and other resources that provide support for advanced programming paradigms. Therefore, the design strategies currently applied to this kind of systems are more focused on solving aspects related to I/O interfacing and/or the fulfilment of real-time requirements rather than solving traditional issues such as the limitation of the capacity or of the resources.

The real-time design methodology described in this paper has been defined as part of the Energos project [1], aimed at providing a smart grid based technology for the management of future electrical distribution networks, using the Data Distribution Service (DDS) [2] middleware as the basis of an enterprise service bus. Execution platforms are typically heterogeneous in this domain. They are constituted by powerful servers installed at the control centres, but also by numerous systems embedded in the remote teleoperation units, in the consumers metering, etc. The main challenge for this kind of embedded system consists in being able of applying high-level software development technologies, seeking for a high degree of modularization in the deployment and reconfiguration processes; but always keeping the capacity to access the physical environment and guaranteeing that the services and responses provided by the system always fulfil its timing requirements.

The usage of Java technology in some sectors of embedded systems development is continuously increasing. Integrating a Java Virtual Machine (JVM) in an embedded system, so that Java can be used as programming language, represents an attractive approach, since the usage of Java brings several advantages: it increases the productivity and the software portability, facilitates the componentization, has a high degree of industrial acceptance, and provides a quick adaptation curve to innovations in software engineering.

The RTSJ (The Real-Time Specification for Java), originally formulated by JSR-1 [3] and currently in revision by JSR-282 [4], and its currently available implementations [5][6] [7], provide Java and the JVM with the resources required for an efficient development of real-time applications oriented to a wide spectrum of industrial domains. Some of these resources are: real-time threads with fixed-priority based schedulers, memory management techniques that guarantee predictability, synchronization mechanisms that avoid priority inversion, efficient management of external events and asynchronous control transfer mechanisms, and a wide set of real-time patterns that are already incorporated in the language [8]. All these aspects provide the capacity to develop hard real-time applications, while keeping the advantages of the Java language mentioned before.

However, designing a real-time application involves not only writing its code, but also configuring its scheduling to guarantee the fulfilment of its specified real-time requirements. Obtaining this scheduling configuration is a really complex task, since it depends on different aspects: the processing capacity required by the application to execute, the processing capacity available in the execution platform, and the workload imposed by the physical environment on the application. Configuring the scheduling of a real-time application requires building a timing analysis model of the application behaviour, which will be used as the basis for applying schedulability analysis techniques and obtaining a suitable scheduling configuration. Formulating this model is not a trivial task even for simple real-time systems, but in the case of applications designed according to an object-oriented (OO) paradigm, as the ones resulting from applying RTSJ, it may present an additional complexity: timing analysis models are typically formulated according to a reactive model, which in the case of an OO application, is usually hidden by the modular architecture of the code. Moreover, obtaining the worst-case execution time (WCET) of the application responses, which is always complex and costly, is also more complex in OO applications. The WCETs depend on several nested invocations among methods of the instances involved, which are hidden by the code and the architecture, and which may vary according to the deployment of the application in the execution platform.

It is not advisable to use testing to verify the schedulability of real-time applications; their timeliness must be certified mathematically as part of the schedulability analysis process, and for doing that, obtaining the analysis model is essential. There are several proposals of frameworks for designing real-time applications with RT-Java, coming from different industrial domains [9][10] [11]. However, they rarely deal with analytical approaches to verify schedulability and subsequently formulate the underlying models. The main difficulty of these models is that they rely on measuring WCET of the code. Although there exist WCET measurement tools for Ada or C code, they can be applied only to relatively simple systems, due to the amount of instrumentation they require. Some of the mechanisms required by Java, such as virtual dispatching and dynamic memory management, are beyond the reach of current tools. A relevant effort to address this problem is presented in [12].

To address these limitations, this work proposes a framework for the design of OO real-time applications based on RT-Java. This framework uses the real-time patterns provided by RTSJ but formalizes their usage, so that the realtime analysis models of the designed applications can be generated automatically according to the specific deployment of the applications in their final execution platforms and without requiring manual analysis of the code. An application developed according to the proposed framework is designed by using a set of systematic and predefined patterns, which allows the code to be automatically instrumented by a tool, as it is shown in Fig. 1. This instrumented code is executed in the configuration mode, i.e. on the final execution embedded platform but in a testing/configuration environment that emulates the real execution environment, forcing the occurrence of all the events that appear in the specification of the application. This testing environment is required since executing the application in its real environment during the configuration phase is not usually possible for this kind of systems, as it will be explained later in the paper. The analysis model is automatically built as a result of this execution in configuration mode. It can then be used as input to a set of schedulability analysis and configuration tools, the ones provided by the MAST environment [13] in our case, which obtain the scheduling configuration that must be applied to the application to make it meet its real-time requirements when it is executed on the final real environment.

The proposed strategy cannot be applied to critical systems with hard real-time requirements, since there is no guarantee that the WCET values obtained are covering the worst-case execution scenario. The measurements are not based on code coverage analysis, examining all their possible paths, but on measurements made during the execution of the system on the emulated configuration environment. This is why, as it is stated in the title of the paper, the proposal is oriented to the design of firm real-time systems ("a task is said to be firm if missing a timing constraint does not jeopardize the correct system behaviour but it is completely useless for the system" [14]), where a certain percentage of missed deadlines is admissible. Hence, this modelling approach is valid for a great variety of industrial applications, excluding critical ones such as avionics, aerospace or nuclear. The main benefit of the approach consists in providing the ability to use advanced programming technologies in non-certified systems.

The paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the framework proposed for the design of real-time OO applications, explaining the RT-Java patterns used. Section III details the formulation of the real-time analysis models that describe the timing behaviour of the applications designed on top of the framework. Section IV explains the instrumentation process carried out to evaluate the real-time model. Finally, the last section summarizes our conclusions.

div.head: APPLICATIONS
div.p: The real-time requirements of an application originate from its interaction with the physical environment in which it operates, which evolves with physical time according to its own dynamics. Hence, a real-time application is specified following a reactive strategy, i.e., describing the responses that it gives to external events coming from the environment, or to timed events received from different system clocks. Thus, specifying a real-time application requires: 1) identifying the events (external or timed) it responds to, 2) specifying the responses, i.e., the sequences of activities that are executed to react to each of the identified events, and 3) specifying the timing requirements that each response must fulfil when it is executed. The activities that belong to a single event response are related by control flow, i.e., an activity starts its execution when the precedent activities in the flow of the response have finished their own execution. On the contrary, activities belonging to different responses are not related by control flow, although synchronization among them may be required if they use a common shared resource that must be accessed with mutual exclusion.

div.head: A. Real-time programming with RT-Java
div.p: RT-Java provides a special kind of thread, NoHeapRealtimeThread, to schedule sequences of activities organized by control flow and with real-time requirements. These threads are executed according to a fixed-priority policy and their execution is not affected by the heap memory management. The main drawback of using them is that every variable or data structure accessed during their execution must be allocated either to immortal memory, which is statically instantiated and cannot be reused, or to scoped memory, which is managed in blocks with a very well-defined lifetime. RT-Java provides a very rich set of patterns to implement responses to events with this type of thread. It provides specialized data types to define the activation patterns (release parameters), the scheduling policies (scheduling parameters), and the memory management schemes (memory parameters) used in the responses.

In RT-Java, as in standard Java, shared resources are associated to instances of classes, guaranteeing mutually exclusive access to the resource for each synchronized method of the class. Oracle RT-Java [6] uses the priority inheritance protocol to control access to the mutex associated to each instance (to each class for static methods). This protocol guarantees the absence of priority inversion.

div.head: B. Modelling-oriented real-time OO framework
div.p: This paper uses the term framework to designate the set of mechanisms defined to support activation, concurrency, flow transfer and mutually exclusive synchronization in the implementation of the real-time responses of the designed applications. Fig. 2 shows the types of responses currently considered in the framework. They could be extended in the future with additional design options, but the proposed set covers the design of many typical real-time applications:
x Responses can be triggered by timed events coming from the system timer (a) or by external events coming from the environment (b).

x If the response has a unique deadline associated to its finalization, and this deadline is smaller than the minimal interarrival time of the triggering event (the period in the case of periodic responses), the response can be scheduled in a single thread (a) (b).

x Responses with intermediate deadlines, or with deadlines larger than the period, may be scheduled on several threads (c). With that aim, the framework provides a synchronization mechanism that is used to transfer the control flow between threads of the same response. x There are applications that require some activities of a response to be executed with bounded jitter, either in the first activity executed after the activation or in the final activity of the response (d). In this case, the framework uses a single thread with varying priority that changes along the execution. Besides, to guarantee the maximum output jitter in the final activity, the execution must be delayed with a specific offset. x Synchronization among responses to different events (e) is supported by means of protected classes (mutexes) and synchronized methods.

x The interaction of real-time responses with activities executed on non real-time subsystems (f) requires mutual exclusion to be implemented in a non-blocking manner for the real-time threads, so that they cannot be suspended in a shared resource by non-real-time activities.

As part of the proposed strategy, a set of stereotypes have been defined to make the role played by each class or method in the reactive model of the application explicit. The roles have been defined by means of stereotypes to preserve the names of classes and methods and the inheritance NoHeapRealtimeThread, which has to be instantiated in scoped or immortal memory. It is responsible for managing the lifecycle of its own provided thread. x «periodicExecutor»: Active class that executes periodically and with a certain configurable priority a task that has been assigned to it. x «boundedJitterPeriodicExecutor»: Specialization of «periodicExecutor» whose assigned task is divided in three subtasks, each one executed with a specific priority, assigned to guarantee the fulfilment of bounded jitter requirements. x «eventHandler»: Active class that executes an infinite loop waiting for a specific event type. When an occurrence of the event is received it executes the task that has been assigned to it, with its configured priority. The bottom part of Fig. 3 shows the stereotypes defined in the framework for methods:
x «executorTask»: Method provided by a «rtTaskJob», which represents the task to be executed by a «periodicExecutor» or an «eventHandler».

x «synchronized»: Method provided by a «protected» class, which is executed in mutual exclusion to any other «synchronized» methods of the same instance. x «entry»: A «synchronized» method provided by an «eventSource» in which the invoking thread may be suspended until the «eventSource» reaches a certain state. Each «eventSource» class has one «entry» at most. x «postWaiting»: Method that represents the section of code of an «entry» method that is executed just after a thread suspended in the «entry» is activated. x «trigger»: A «synchronized» method of a «synchronizer» class that is invoked by a thread, causing the state change that can activate the suspended threads (if any). x «waitFreeSynchronized»: A «synchronized» nonblocking method of a «waitFreeProtected» class. Fig. 4 represents a real-time object-oriented application, used as an example in this paper. The application is executed on an embedded computer that supervises a three-phase line breaker of an electric power distribution substation. The figure shows the subsystems and modules that form the application, the four responses that it implements, and the real-time requirements that must be satisfied. For the purpose of the paper, the specific electrical functionality of the application is not relevant, so it is not shown. The «rtTaskJob» Metrology class provides the main functionality required for implementing this response. It is not a simple class, because it is comprised of a set of passive classes that provide specific functionalities. The first activity in the response (corresponding to updating metrology data) has a hard deadline of 200 ms, which is the minimum time required to avoid overriding the waveform data. On the contrary, the second activity (publishing the perturbation data in the data space) has no real-time requirements.

The code that is executed periodically, and as a consequence whose execution time must be measured, is encapsulated in the update method provided by Metrology (stereotyped as «executorTask»). On the other hand, the thread that schedules the section of the response that has real-time requirements is provided by MetrologyExecutor, which is a nested class of Metrology and stereotyped as «periodicExecutor». The activity of the response aimed at transferring data to the DDS space does not have timing requirements. Thus, it is scheduled by a second thread with lower priority that is provided by the «eventHandler» PertubographExecutor class. Transfer of control between both threads is carried out by means of the «synchronizer» Perturbogram class.

The thread introduced by PertubographExecutor suspends itself in the «entry» awaitPerturbogram method of Perturbogram until the thread corresponding to MetrologyExecutor invokes the «trigger» finalized method, which activates the suspended thread. The interaction of the second thread (the one provided by MetrologyExecutor) with the DDS publisher, which is non-realtime, is made through the «waitFreeSynchronized» submitPerturbogram method that guarantees the execution of the method with mutual exclusion, but without blocking the invoking thread if the mutex is already held by a non-realtime thread. If this happens, the invoking thread keeps the information for the next invocation. A sequence diagram modelling the sequence of activities that constitute the MetrologyUpdating response is shown in Fig. 6.

div.head: III. REAL-TIME MODEL OF THE RT-JAVA SYSTEM
div.p: In our case, the real-time model used to configure the scheduling of the application, i.e., to obtain the set of values that must be assigned to the threads involved in the real-time responses of the application, is formulated according to the MAST modelling methodology [13]. A MAST analysis model is divided in three complementary sections:

div.head: A. Platform model
div.p: The platform model describes the processing capacity available for executing the application by the processors of the embedded system. It also describes the fraction of this capacity that is consumed by background activities (such as the scheduler and the system timer management). Fig. 7 shows the MAST model corresponding to an Oracle/Sun Java RTS 2.2 platform installed on Ubuntu Linux 2.6.X.rt [15]. This example has a single-processor execution platform, so only one MAST::Regular_Processor element is included in the model. The scheduler applies a fixed priority policy with a priority range from 11 to 58 that is defined by the JVM. Priorities lower than 11 belong to non-real-time Java threads. The context switch times of the scheduler depend on the specific processor so they must be measured for each platform used. RTSJ uses two Linux timers. The first one, modelled by rtTimer, is a real-time timer of the type alarm clock, i.e., it only consumes CPU when a thread is suspended or activated. It provides high accuracy (1.5 μs). The second timer (nrtTimer) is the Java standard one and is of the ticker type, meaning that it generates events periodically (period = 1 ms). The latter one is not used in real-time applications, but the CPU usage due to its activations must be taken into account in the model, to analyse schedulability.

div.head: B. Logical model
div.p: The logical model describes the execution times of the relevant methods of the application. When using the reference model proposed, there are two kinds of methods whose timing behaviour model must be evaluated and modelled:

x The methods with stereotype «synchronized» (and its subclasses). They are executed with mutual exclusion on the instances of «protected» classes, so as a consequence, their invoking threads can be blocked upon them. The «waitFreeSynchronized» methods do not need to be modelled since they cannot cause blocking to real-time threads. The model of a «synchronized» method is composed of a MAST::Priority_Inheritance_Mutex element, which models the mutex that Java associates to each «protected» class; and a MAST::Simple_Operation element, which models the execution time of the method and references the mutexes required, indicating that the method is executed with mutual exclusion. The model of a single method of a «protected» class is different for each instance of the class, since for each instance there is a corresponding mutex instance and the execution times could be different. x The methods stereotyped as «executorTask», which define the tasks executed by the threads that schedule the real-time responses. These methods are modelled as MAST::Enclosing_Operation elements, which describe the total execution time of the methods when they are executed without being preempted from the scheduler or blocked in the access to protected methods. An Enclosing_Operation includes also the list of all the protected methods that may be invoked during its execution. For more details about the semantics of this element see [12]. The model of an «executorTask» method must also be established per instance.

x As an example of logical model, Fig. 8 shows the MAST model of the «executorTask» submit method of an instance of the Perturbograph class. The corresponding Enclosing_Operation describes its worst, average and best case execution times, and the two protected methods invoked during its execution. The Priority_ Inheritance_Mutex element models the mutex associated to the instance of the Perturbogram protected class, and the two Simple_Operation elements model the awaitPerturbogram and marshall «synchronized» methods. For traceability purposes, the identifier of each element of the MAST model is generated so that it includes the Java identifier (e.g. 2AE3 or 3FAB) of the instance the methods belong to.

The logical model of an object-oriented application may be composed of a huge number of modelling elements, whose formulation requires carrying out several measurements of execution times. For example, the logical model of the MetrologyUpdating response involves 2 Enclosing_Operation, 41 Simple_Operation and 19 Priority_Inheritance_Mutex elements. This is where the real benefit of the proposed framework is obtained, since it helps to simplify the process of formulation of the logical model.

div.head: C. Reactive model of the application
div.p: This model defines the elements that describe the realtime responses specified in the application functionality and relates them with the rest of the elements of the model. Fig. 9 shows the model for a response, including:

x A set of MAST::Thread elements that model the threads into which the response is scheduled (e.g., 42CF.Metrology Executor.thread). Each one includes the model of the scheduling parameters of the thread as an aggregated element (42CF.SchedParam).

x The model of the response formulated by means of a MAST::End_To_End_Flow (42CF.MetrologyExecutor.Metro-logyUpdating), which includes as aggregations the MAST::Workload_Event, MAST::Step and MAST:: Internal_Event elements that describe, respectively, the activation pattern, the activities executed, and the states

div.head: trigger). Each
div.p: Step (e.g. 42CF.step2) models an activity of the response by relating the operation executed (2AE3.Perturbograph.submit), which contains the execution time and is part of the logical model (see Fig. 8), with the thread that executes it (11A2.Perturbograph.thread), and the input (42CF.e1) and output (42CF.e2) events that define the control flow. When a certain event occurrence has a timing requirement associated, the corresponding event model (e.g. 42CF.e1) has an aggregated MAST::Hard_ Global_Deadline element (42CF.ghd) that specifies the deadline that must be met.

Once the real-time model of the application is formulated, the MAST environment provides several tools aimed at certifying its schedulability or at calculating the priorities that must be assigned to the threads to make the application schedulable. If the MAST tools are not able to find a configuration that makes the application schedulable, MAST also provides a sensitivity analysis tool that can be used to assess how close or far is the system from schedulability. This information is essential to decide the modifications that must be applied to the reactivity, the structure or the implementation of the application to make it meet its real-time requirements.

div.head: IV. INSTRUMENTATION OF THE APPLICATION CODE FOR AUTOMATIC EXTRACTION OF THE REAL-TIME MODEL
div.p: This section addresses the automatic generation of the MAST model that will be used for the schedulability analysis and configuration of an application designed according to the framework proposed. The generation process relies on tags added to the Java source code of the application. All the elements that play a key role in the real-time model are tagged according to their nature. The tags follow the format @oort«xxx», where «xxx» is a string that identifies the nature of the element. These tags are placed in the line above the element declaration. The defined tags appear in Table 1. As expected, they correspond to the stereotypes defined in the framework and shown before.

div.head: TABLE I. TAGS USED IN THE GENERATION OF THE TIMING MODEL
Class tags
div.p: Method tags @oortPeriodicExecutor @oortEventHandler @oortBoundedJitterExecutor @oortProtected @oortEventSource @oortSynchronizer @oortProtected @oortEntry @oortPostWait @oortTrigger @oortMain As it was shown in Fig. 1, the model generation is carried out in two steps:

1) The source code of the application (appropriately tagged) is processed by a tool that generates a new Java project with the instrumented code. The approach followed for the code instrumentation consists of inserting within the code, invocations to a set of static methods provided by the OORTTimeMntr class, whose specification is shown in Fig. 10 and which is used with three different purposes.
First, to register the creation of each instance of the tagged classes and their corresponding methods. The following methods are used with that aim:

x OORTTimeMntr() initializes the data structure that is required to register and monitor all the instances that form the application; it is invoked from the main() method of the application in the configuration environment. x createProtectedObject() creates the data structure used to register and monitor an instance of a protected class (@oortProtected tag); it must be invoked from the protected object constructor. x createdSynchrOperMntr() creates the data structure that registers the data needed to calculate the execution time of the associated protected method, and the pid that univocally identifies each invoking thread; it must be invoked from the constructor of the protected object, once for each protected operation declared in it. x createThreadMntr() creates the data structure that is used to monitor the execution time of a thread (instance of classes with @oortPeriodicExecutor, @oortEventHandler or @oortBoundedJitterPeriodicExecutor tags); it must be invoked by the monitored thread itself. The last two methods return an integer index that identifies the data structure created, which must be later referenced by the methods used to measure and register the execution times (through the src argument).

Once all these data structures are created, the OORTTimeMntr class is used to measure time intervals by means of a thread timer (i.e., a timer that measures the time that the thread to which it is associated is scheduled for execution). Since the RT-Java version used (RTS 2.1 from Oracle) does not provide thread timers, the framework uses timers from the OS that are accessed by means of native invocations (JNI). The methods used with that aim are: x recordThreadTime(), which registers the execution time of the task associated to a thread; it must be invoked once for each cycle of execution of the task associated to a «periodicExecutor» or an «eventHandler». x recordOperationTime() measures the time elapsed between two consecutive invocations of this method; it must be invoked at the start and finish point of each invocation of a protected method.

Table II shows as an example of instrumented code the skeleton of the PerturbographExecutor class. The tag in a) indicates that the following class is an «eventHandler». The structure used to monitor the behaviour of each instance of this class is created in c). The identifier returned from the creation is stored in the peSrc variable, which is declared in b). It will be used to access the data structure to store 2) The instrumented application is executed in the configuration environment, but in a platform identical to the embedded platform used in the real environment. This emulated environment is required because during the configuration (modelling) process the responses of the application to all events that the real environment can generate must be characterized (even those that occur occasionally). When this configuration execution has finished executing, the OORTTimeMntr is used to generate the real-time model of the application by invoking generateMastModel() at the end of the main() method of the application. This method uses the information that has been stored in the OORTTimeMntr instance during the execution to:
x Identify the threads that initiate responses.

x Identify the threads that execute internal parts of a response, and relate them to the previous and subsequent threads in the control flow. x Identify and characterize the task executed by each thread, assigning it the measured execution times and aggregating to it the protected methods that are invoked during its execution. x Identify and characterize the protected methods, assigning them their measured execution times.

Based on these identified elements, the logical and reactive part of the corresponding MAST model can be generated. To complete the model, the operator must introduce the information describing the execution platform and the environment workload, which cannot be extracted from executing the application.

V. CONCLUSIONS Addressing the software complexity of current embedded systems with firm real-time requirements requires applying advanced programming paradigms, such as object-oriented or component-based approaches. There are some programming languages, such as Ada and RT-Java, which together with their associated run-time technologies, provide the ability to add real-time features to object-oriented programming. However, the correct execution of a real-time application requires the code to be executed with a suitable scheduling configuration. Obtaining this configuration requires a characterization of the timing behaviour of the application when it is instantiated on an embedded platform. In the case of complex object-oriented applications, formulating the real-time model used to apply schedulability analysis and obtain a suitable scheduling configuration is a complex and tedious task that must be carried out for each of the different configurations of the application, for each embedded platform in which it is going to be executed, and for each workload imposed by the external environment. This paper proposes a design framework that simplifies this scheduling configuration process when dealing with RT-Java object-oriented applications.

x «rtTaskJob»: Passive class that acts as a container for the resources used by the tasks that are executed by a «periodicExecutor» or an «eventHandler». x «protected»: Passive class that represents a shared resource that must be accessed with mutual exclusion. x «waitFreeProtected»: Extension of «protected» that guarantees non-blocking access to the shared resource. It is used in the interaction among real-time and non realtime activities. x «eventSource»: Passive class that manages the reception of events. It provides the synchronization mechanisms required to suspend a thread until the next occurrence of the specific event that the thread attends. x «synchronizer»: Passive class in which threads can be suspended waiting for a state change. The state change is produced synchronously by an invocation made by another thread (in the same class). It constitutes the mechanism used to transfer control flow among threads executing different activities of the same response.
